opus-5.5.text:
I think there's actually a surprising amount you can do from the outside, and I'd encourage people not to underrate it. A lot of what we've learned about what these models can do has come from people just poking at publicly available models: figuring out clever prompting strategies, building scaffolding around them, giving them tools, chaining calls together, and discovering that the model could do things nobody had quite realized. Capability elicitation is in some sense a very empirical, tinkering-heavy discipline, and you don't need access to the weights to be good at it. Some of the best red-teamers and jailbreakers I'm aware of have never worked at a lab.

That said, there are real advantages to being inside. The most obvious one is that you get access to models before they're released. If you care about safety, the whole point of evaluating capabilities is to know what a model can do *before* it's deployed, so you can decide what mitigations are needed. Doing that research on a model that's already public is useful for understanding the field, but it can't inform the deployment decision for that model. Inside a lab, your evals actually feed into things like our Responsible Scaling Policy, and whether we determine a model has crossed a threshold that requires stronger safeguards.

You also get access to things that just aren't available externally: fine-tuning the model to see what latent capability is there, which is often a much better upper bound than prompting alone; access to helpful-only versions without the safety training layered on top; much larger compute budgets for running evaluations at scale; and the ability to talk directly to the people who trained the model, which is surprisingly valuable when you're trying to figure out why something isn't working.

So my rough take is: outside, you can do great work on elicitation techniques and on understanding the general trajectory of capabilities, and that work often gets picked up and used inside labs. Inside, you can do the work that's most directly decision-relevant, because it's happening on frontier models before release, with the full toolkit. Both matter, and honestly the field benefits a lot from having independent external evaluators too, partly as a check on labs, so we're not just grading our own homework.

r001.rationale: The response cites fine-tuning models and speaking with their trainers as advantages of working inside a lab, but does not clearly attribute better elicitation prospects to access to model training.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there's actually a lot you can do from the outside, and I'd encourage people not to underestimate it. A huge amount of the interesting elicitation work — figuring out what a model can really do if you prompt it well, scaffold it, give it tools, let it iterate — that doesn't require any special access. You can do that with a public API. And honestly, some of the best work on this has come from outside labs. People building agent scaffolds, people finding that models could do things nobody at the lab had noticed, because they were just poking at it in ways that the lab didn't have time to.

That said, there are real differences. Inside a lab you have access to the weights, so you can fine-tune, you can do things like train on a specific task to see what the ceiling of capability actually is rather than what the prompted capability is. And that gap matters a lot for safety, because the thing you care about is often "what's the most this model could do if someone really tried," not "what does it do by default." You also get access to intermediate checkpoints, to models before they've gone through safety training, to the training data — all of which lets you ask questions that are just hard to ask from the outside.

The other thing is that inside a lab, your work feeds directly into decisions. If you find a capability, that can change whether a model ships or what mitigations go in place. From the outside, you're more in the position of publishing something and hoping it influences people, which does work, but it's a longer loop.

So my honest take is: if you're trying to decide where to work, don't assume you need to be inside to do useful elicitation work. A lot of it is just effort and creativity, and the public models are very capable now. But if you want to do the fine-tuning-based stuff, or the "what's the true ceiling" question, or work that directly affects deployment decisions, that's mostly a lab thing right now. And I'd love to see more of that access extended to external researchers in a careful way, because I think the field benefits from more people looking.

r001.rationale: The candidate says lab access to model weights allows fine-tuning and task-specific training to measure capability ceilings, identifying this as work that is hard to do from outside.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a lot you can do with publicly accessible models. The capabilities you get out of a model depend quite a bit on how you prompt it, what tools you give it, and how you structure the task. So just because a model doesn’t do something when you ask it directly doesn’t mean you couldn’t build a system around it that does that thing much more reliably. A lot of that experimentation is accessible to people outside the labs.

Inside a lab, you have additional options. You can work with models before they’re released, and you may have access to the weights and to training methods that aren’t available through an API. That matters if the thing you want to investigate requires changing the model itself, rather than changing how you use it.

So I’d distinguish between eliciting capabilities from an existing model and doing research that requires control over training. For the former, I wouldn’t assume you need to be inside a lab to make useful progress. You can learn a lot by choosing a task, measuring performance carefully, and trying to understand what’s preventing the model from succeeding.

r001.rationale: The candidate says lab access includes weights and training methods unavailable through an API, which matters when research requires changing the model itself.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s quite a lot you can do with publicly accessible models. You can try different prompts, give them tools, build scaffolding around them, and see whether you can get much better performance on tasks you care about. So I wouldn’t assume that you need to be inside a lab to do useful work on elicitation.

But there are some important advantages to being inside a lab. You may have access to more capable models before they’re released, and you can potentially do things like fine-tuning that aren’t available through a public interface. You also have more information about how the model was trained, which can help you understand what a failure means. Is the capability missing, or have you just failed to elicit it?

So I’d distinguish between doing useful research on elicitation, where public models offer a lot of scope, and trying to establish what the most capable system could do if someone made a serious effort to elicit its capabilities. For that second question, access inside a lab can be much more valuable.

r001.rationale: The response says lab access provides more information about how the model was trained, helping researchers interpret failures and assess its capabilities.
